hints: Compare the formula of benzophenone, $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, with T, $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$, to work out what small alkyl fragment has been added in step 2.
Look at the structure after step 3 and after step 4 to deduce what functional group must have been present on the side chain in T and in U before those changes.
walkthrough:
Read T from its formula and its neighbour**
Think of benzophenone as $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5$. T has formula $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$, so it has gained $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ overall. That is exactly what happens when one ring H is replaced by an ethyl group, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. So T must be an ethyl-substituted benzophenone.

Fix the position and confirm with step 3**
Now look ahead. Step 3 gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$. That product comes from bromination of an ethyl side chain at the benzylic position. So T must contain $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ on the second ring, in the 3-position (meta to the $\text{C=O}$) as in ketoprofen: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Read U by working backwards from ketoprofen**
Ketoprofen ends with $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Step 5 converts U into that acid. The classic route from alkyl bromide to acid is bromide to nitrile to acid. Since step 3 made $\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$, step 4 must replace $\text{Br}$ by $\text{CN}$. So U is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CN}$.

Final answer: T is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (3-ethylbenzophenone, meta isomer).
U is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CN}$ (the corresponding benzylic nitrile).

hints: For step 1, benzene to benzophenone adds a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}$ group, think which acyl chloride plus $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst gives this Friedel-Crafts acylation.
For step 2, benzophenone to ethylbenzophenone adds an ethyl group to the ring, think which chloroalkane plus $\text{AlCl}_3$ gives this Friedel-Crafts alkylation.
For step 3, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$ is selective benzylic substitution, think which reagent with light or heat gives free radical bromination.
For step 4, $\text{R-Br}$ to $\text{R-CN}$ replaces Br by CN, think which cyanide source in ethanolic solution with heat gives nucleophilic substitution.
For step 5, $\text{R-CN}$ to $\text{R-CO}_2\text{H}$ adds two molecules of water across the triple bond, think which aqueous acid with boiling under reflux gives complete hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Step 1, making the ketone bridge**
You start from benzene and make $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COC}_6\text{H}_5$. That is joining a second phenyl ring through a $\text{C=O}$. The standard A Level way is Friedel-Crafts acylation using benzoyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$, with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst, with warming. The $\text{AlCl}_3$ generates the strong electrophile $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}^+\text{=O}$.

Step 2, adding the ethyl group**
Next you add $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to the ring. That is Friedel-Crafts alkylation using chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst, with heat. Do not use ethane or ethene here, the electrophile must come from a halogenoalkane with the Lewis acid catalyst.

Step 3, brominating the side chain only**
Here $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ becomes $\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$. The ring is untouched and the ketone is untouched. This is free radical substitution at the benzylic position, which is very susceptible to radical attack. Use bromine, $\text{Br}_2$, with UV light (or strong heat). No $\text{AlCl}_3$ or $\text{FeBr}_3$, because that would cause ring bromination.

Step 4, swapping Br for CN**
Here $\text{R-Br}$ becomes $\text{R-CN}$. Cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$, is a good nucleophile for a benzylic secondary bromide. Use KCN or NaCN, warmed in ethanol. Ethanol is important because it dissolves both the organic bromide and the ionic cyanide. Aqueous conditions alone would favour substitution to an alcohol.

Step 5, turning nitrile into acid**
Here $\text{R-CN}$ becomes $\text{R-CO}_2\text{H}$, which is ketoprofen. This is complete acid hydrolysis of a nitrile, which needs vigorous conditions. Use dilute aqueous acid such as HCl(aq) or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$(aq), i.e. $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, with heat, boiling under reflux. Alkaline hydrolysis followed by acidification also works chemically, but the mark scheme expects acid and heat.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ + $\text{AlCl}_3$ (+ heat)
step 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ + $\text{AlCl}_3$ (+ heat)
step 3: $\text{Br}_2$ + light (or heat)
step 4: KCN (or NaCN) + heat in ethanol
step 5: $\text{H}^+$ / $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ e.g. dilute HCl(aq) or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$(aq) + heat / boil / reflux

hints: For step 1, recall the general name for any Friedel-Crafts reaction on benzene where an electrophile replaces a ring H.
For step 5, recall the general name for splitting a molecule with water, here $\text{R-CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R-CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$.
walkthrough:
Classify step 1**
Picture benzene donating its pi electrons to a strong positive electrophile, then losing $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity. That pattern is electrophilic substitution. Step 1 is the acylation example of it.

Classify step 5**
Picture $\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$ reacting with two molecules of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{R-COOH}$ plus ammonia or ammonium ion. Breaking bonds with water in this way is hydrolysis. It can also be viewed as nucleophilic substitution by water at the nitrile carbon, so that name is also accepted.

Final answer: step 1: electrophilic substitution (Friedel-Crafts acylation)
step 5: hydrolysis (acid hydrolysis, also acceptable as nucleophilic substitution)
